name: Pulaar
confidence_why: Niang 1995, a native speaker's study devoted to Pulaar stress, sets out the weight-sensitive system (main stress on the heaviest non-final syllable, CVVC > CVV > CVC > CV, first syllable by default) that Wiltshire 2006 and McLaughlin & Wiltshire 2017 adopt, and the only dissent, a hedged, page-less excerpt from Anyanwu & Diallo 2007 saying the first syllable of "Fula" words is stressed "irrespective of length", comes from a chapter about accent mobility whose co-author's variety is Guinean Pular, so it most likely describes a different variety or a default that the chapter then qualifies.

sweep_summary: Pulaar (pula1263) is coded 'weight' from Niang 1995 (KWPL 20), and nothing found in this search of works with stress in the title moves that. Five target items: (1) Wiltshire 2006 (open Cascadilla PDF, held by the project and read) restates Niang 1997 exactly as the catalog has it (heaviest non-final syllable CVVC>CVV>CVC>CV, leftmost on ties, initial default, final never stressed except monosyllables) — confirms. (2) Niang 1995 is the catalog's own deciding source (Glottolog 'already_listed=false' is a bibliography gap); copied into our files and re-read — confirms. (3) Prunet 1989 (CAAL 6, De Gruyter DOI 10.1515/9783110884890-010, paywalled): the Google Books opening snippet shows it is an analysis of the voice/aspect system via length 'redistribution', and a search-within of the volume for 'stress' has no hit in pp. 138-160 — prosody-but-not-word-stress, silent, low priority. (4) Anyanwu & Diallo (FAB 17: 65-89, Köppe, paywalled): a Google Books snippet reads 'In Fula, it is primary stress that is more relevant. Generally, the first syllable of the word receives the stress, irrespective of length' — potentially in tension with weight-sensitivity, but the paper (title: 'word accent mobility') was not read and the variety is probably Guinean Pular (Diallo's specialty), so relevance to pula1263 is unclear; high priority to acquire. (5) Zubko 1973 (Russian, Olderogge Festschrift p. 396ff; title supplied from a Google Books TOC snippet, Glottolog has it 'wanting'): print only, content unread, medium priority. Extra find: McLaughlin & Wiltshire 2017 'Syllable weight in the phonology of Pulaar' (Benjamins, DOI 10.1075/cilt.338.10lau, paywalled; snippets restate the Niang/Wiltshire generalisations for Mauritanian/Fuutankoore Pulaar) — worth adding to the bibliography. searches ran by automated download (Crossref, Glottolog, Google Books feed, Köppe, kunstkamera); All downloaded records and are under

This is the same system the catalog codes from Niang 1995 (weight, default initial), now with the monosyllable exception and secondary-stress rule stated explicitly. It is a restatement of Niang 1997, not independent fieldwork, so it corroborates rather than replaces the deciding source.

new_statements.quote: [p. 22, § 15] Nach § 11 soll im Handbuch das Starktonzeichen nur gesetzt werden, wenn eine andere als die vorletzte Silbe des Wortes vom Starkton getroffen wird. Wäre ēu in der Form rēuɓe „Frauen“ des Handbuchs nach § 5 daselbst „nicht einsilbig“, also nicht ein Diphthong, dann müßte ja das u des Wortes den Gipfel der vorletzten Silbe bilden und das Wort selbst also, da ohne Akzentzeichen, rēúɓe zu betonen sein. [p. 58 n. 1] ... in der Form wapańēɓe Poular II S. 214 zu belegen, in der ich ē als — durch den Pänultima-Akzent gedehnten — Sproßvokal auffasse.
new_statements.translation: [p. 22] According to § 11 of the Handbuch [Westermann 1909, Handbuch der Ful-Sprache] the strong-stress mark is set only when a syllable other than the penultimate syllable of the word carries the main stress. If ēu in the Handbuch's form rēuɓe 'women' were, per its § 5, 'not monosyllabic', i.e. not a diphthong, then the u would have to form the peak of the penultimate syllable and the word itself, having no accent mark, would have to be stressed rēúɓe. [p. 58 n. 1] ... attested in the form wapańēɓe, Poular II [Gaden 1914, Le Poular, dialecte peul du Fouta sénégalais] p. 214, in which I take ē to be an epenthetic vowel lengthened by the penultimate accent.

new_statements.relation_note: Placement differs: the catalog codes Pulaar as weight-sensitive with initial default (Niang 1995; Wiltshire 2006 after Niang 1997) and Anyanwu & Diallo give initial stress for Fula, whereas this work takes a penultimate accent as the Ful norm (Westermann 1909 convention for Sokoto/Hausa-states Ful; Klingenheben's own 'Pänultima-Akzent' applied to a Gaden Fouta-Sénégalais form). The disagreement is weak evidence: the remarks are incidental, partly second-hand, mostly about Nigerian Fulfulde rather than Pulaar, and the one Pulaar example (wa.pa.ńē.ɓe, long penult) would also receive penult stress under Niang's heaviest-syllable rule. It documents the older (pre-Arnott) penult-accent view of F…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The book is a comparative segmental phonology (sound inventory, Proto-Ful, dialect sound changes) with no section on accent or tone. Word stress enters only incidentally: Klingenheben reports Westermann's transcription convention for the Ful of the Hausa states, under which main stress ('Starkton') on the penultimate syllable is the unmarked default and a stress mark is written only when some other syllable is stressed; and in a footnote he himself invokes 'the penultimate accent' as the force that lengthened an epenthetic vowel in the Fouta-Sénégalais (Pulaar) form wapańēɓe from Gaden. So the work presupposes a penultimate word accent in Ful as the normal case, with lexically marked departures (Westermann's marked forms), without analysing it.
new_statements.exceptions: Implicit only: Westermann's Handbuch marks the words whose stress is not penultimate (no list or rule given here). § 108 n. 2 (p. 140) merely lists 'Akzent (im weitesten Sinne)' among possible conditioning factors of sound change.
new_statements.identity_note: The work treats Ful as a whole: Part I is explicitly 'Der Lautbestand des Ful der Hausastaaten' (Sokoto/Adamawa, i.e. Nigerian Fulfulde, after Westermann 1909/1913), Parts II-IV draw on Futa Jallon (Reichardt, Arensdorff), Fouta Sénégalais = Pulaar (Gaden 1913-14 'Poular I/II'), Masina, Adamaua, Bagirmi sources. The p. 22 stress remark is about Westermann's Hausa-states Ful; the p. 58 'Pänultima-Akzent' remark is applied to a Pulaar (Fouta Sénégalais) form from Gaden.

readall_conflicts: One disagreement, snippet-level only: the Google Books snippet from Anyanwu & Diallo 2007 ('Generally, the first syllable of the word receives the stress, irrespective of length') describes weight-insensitive initial stress, whereas the catalog and the existing Niang 1995/1997 and Wiltshire 2006 statements make Pulaar weight-sensitive (heaviest non-final syllable, CVVC > CVV > CVC > CV, initial only when all syllables are CV or on ties). The snippet has no page, is hedged with 'Generally', comes from a chapter titled 'word accent mobility' (which may go on to describe weight-driven shifts), and Diallo's Fula is Guinean Pular, so the conflict may be a variety difference or an opening generalisation rather than a true contradiction. The full chapter (pp. 65-89, paid PDF from Köppe) is needed to settle it. The three works actually read (Peace Corps 1993, Barbot 1732) are silent; Labatut and Klingenheben could not be opened. Klingenheben 1927 (incidentally, pp. 22 and 58) presupposes a penultimate word accent in Ful, following Westermann 1909's convention that stress is marked only when it is not on the penult; the catalog record (Niang 1995) and Wiltshire 2006 describe Pulaar stress as weight-driven with an initial default and never final, and Anyanwu & Diallo describe Fula stress as initial. The 1927 remarks are not an analysis, have no accent section behind them, concern chiefly the Ful of the Hausa states (Nigerian Fulfulde) with one Fouta-Sénégalais example whose long penul…

sources.quote: Generalizations The last syllable of the word is never stressed. Stress the first syllable if there is no heavy syllable in the word as in (7). [...] Stress the penult syllable if it is the only heavy syllable in the word as in (8). [...] When both first and penult syllables have the same structure CVC, CVV or CVVC, stress the first syllable as in (9). [...] When both first and penult syllables are heavy but with different weight, stress the heaviest syllable. CVVC is heavier than CVV which in turn is heavier than CVC which is heavier than CV as in (10).
sources.note: This is the catalog's deciding source, re-read: final syllable extrametrical, heaviest non-final syllable wins on a four-way scale, leftmost on ties, initial default. p. 53 also summarises earlier Fula accounts (Taylor 1953: stress depends on long vowels; Arnott 1970: first syllable salient; McIntosh 1984: last non-final CVC/CVV else initial; Prunet & Tellier 1984: first heavy syllable from the left, else initial). Glottolog's 'already_listed=false' is a bibliography bookkeeping gap: the work is our deciding source.

sources.locator: Google Books snippet of the chapter opening (p. 138); Google Books search-within of the volume for 'stress'
sources.note: Judging from the opening snippet, the paper is an analysis of the Fula voice/aspect (verbal) system in terms of 'prosodic redistribution' of skeletal length (vowel length / consonant gemination; cf. Prunet & Tellier 1984 on Pulaar vowel shortening, and the same chapter title in Prunet's 1992 McGill thesis 'Spreading and Locality Domains in Phonology'). A Google Books search-within of the volume for 'stress' returns hits on pp. 19-60 and p. 284 but none in pp. 138-160, so the chapter appears not to discuss stress placement.
